artifact.prose:
Wind drove rain through the open lighthouse door. Ekin stood beside Duru in the upper room, with the cat-sized hatchling crouched near them. Below, seawater surged through the grate and washed across the lower room.

A broad shadow crossed the doorway.

The mother sea dragon pushed her head and shoulders into the upper room, unable to force the rest of her body through the narrow way. Ekin tensed, but Duru stayed still. The hatchling scrambled forward.

The sea dragon curved her neck around the little dragon, sheltering it from the rain and wind. One wing pressed across the doorway while the hatchling tucked itself safely beneath her. Mother and hatchling remained together in the dry upper room.

Ekin and Duru watched. The dragon did not look at them for approval. Her attention stayed on the hatchling.

Ekin glanced toward the stormy sea. Somewhere beneath those dark waves, Grandfather’s brass compass was gone. The thought hurt as sharply as before, but she no longer moved toward the stairs.

“I’m not getting it back,” she said.

Duru looked at her, waiting.

Ekin swallowed. “I know. It’s lost.”

Duru gave a small nod. “Then we should take the coastal route while it’s still passable.”

Ekin’s first answer rose to her lips—an angry refusal, out of habit. Another blast shook rain against the lighthouse. She looked at Duru, then at the sheltered hatchling.

“All right,” she said. “You lead where the ground is worst. I’ll stay with you.”

They left the dragons in the upper room and stepped onto the known coastal route together.

The storm followed them all the way. Rain stung their faces, wind shoved at their shoulders, and the sea crashed below the headland. Duru chose each turn, but she never hurried beyond Ekin’s reach. When the gusts struck hardest, Ekin matched her pace instead of arguing.

They reached the harbor soaked and tired, still side by side. The storm had not ended, and the compass had not returned. But when Duru pointed out the safer ground ahead, Ekin listened.
